newsitem.title: USA: NJ Senate needs more time to weigh pension bonds.
newsitem.headline: NJ Senate needs more time to weigh pension bonds.

text.p: - Gov Christie Whitman's plan to sell $2.75 billion of pension obligation bonds stalled in the state Senate Thursday, and some senators questioned if it could be approved in time to help balance the next budget.

The senate began its voting session late Thursday afternoon with the issue still unresolved. The Republican majority resumed deliberations in caucus at 1800 EDT, after voting for other bills on the agenda.

A solid phalanx of Democratic opposition, joined by a handful of Republican senators, has stymied the proposal, which would enable the administration to avoid $590 million in pension payments through June 1998.
Several senators have said they could not vote for a bill that endangered the state's credit rating. Earlier this week, S&P softened its warning, but that did not move the opposition.

Another obstacle is that tax revenues are coming in far above budget projections. The Whitman administration puts the cushion at more than $200 million, but the Office of Legislative Services estimated revenues at $494 million, and there was speculation even that total was conservative.

There was strong sentiment within the Republican majority that it would be better to wait until closer to the June 30 deadline for approving a balanced budget. Whitman proposed a $16.2 billion spending plan for the new fiscal year that starts July 1.
"There is a date certain by which we have to pass the bond issue or find an alternative route to balanced budget, but June 5th is not that date," said state Senator Joseph Kyrillos, R- Middlesex.

The governor's chief counsel, Michael Torpey, was lobbying for action Thursday. He pointed out that the state was due to make a $200 million pension payment within days, and once paid, that money cannot be recovered. A previous administration had drawn IRS scrutiny of a pension maneuver that enabled it to recover funds already paid into the four funds.

Whitman said last week her plan was needed to provide up to $250 million to achieve the level of state aid the state Supreme Court ordered May 14 for 28 poor school districts. The Supreme Court rejected Whitman's argument that setting core curriculum standards lessened the need for equal spending power.

In 1990, the high court identified 28 districts it said had special needs, and in 1994 it ordered New Jersey to equalize its per pupil spending with the average of the state's most affluent districts by September 1997. Its latest order held Whitman to that deadline, ruling that her reforms were helpful but not sufficient.

The Gov's original pension bond plan called for borrowing $3.4 billion, which would have enabled her to forgo $647 million in contributions to the state's four funds. The state Senate pared down the proposal, reducing its budget benefit to $590 million. There was speculation the plan would have to be further reduced to get a majority of state Republicans to agree to it.
